feedback: If the child places shapes at random and names the result only afterwards, do not mark this wrong — it is an expected early level. Offer a challenge one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
If the child names only the whole ('a rocket') but not the parts, take the composite apart and name each solid together, then rebuild it, naming each shape as it goes on.

If the tower topples, look together at which faces rest on the table or on the shape below: a sphere rolls because it has no flat face, a cone balanced on its point has no flat face down, and a piece placed off-centre can tip over. So choose a flat-faced solid (a cube, prism, or cylinder on a flat face) for the base, keep each piece centred, and don't stack anything on a cone's point, rather than blaming the blocks.
Reinforce correct anticipation: when the child reaches for the cone before placing it, confirm the plan aloud ('yes — the cone fits on top of the cylinder').
activities.intendedInsight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.
learnerActions: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids

feedback: If the challenge is too hard, step back one level and rebuild success before advancing again.
Praise the planning talk ('I'll put the cone on top next'), not just the finished structure.
activities.intendedInsight: Children advance most when the next task is just ahead of their current building, with support that fades, rather than jumping straight to the final target.
learnerActions: Watch how the child currently builds to judge their level (free stacking, trial-and-error assembly, or anticipating).
Set a building challenge just one step beyond that level — for example, from stacking identical cubes to combining a cone on a cylinder, or from trial-and-error assembly to predicting the next piece.
Scaffold with prompts and modelling, then gradually fade support as the child succeeds.
Repeat the same build and ask the child to say each shape as they add it.
activities.title: Challenges pitched one level ahead
